phonemes.desc: Voiced velar stop with close front vowel [ɡil] — firm, like the name of a builder.
The second velar with open [a] — the name's hinge.
Final [mɛʃ] — the hushing sibilant š, 'sh' as in 'ship', the sound the ASCII spelling loses.

pronunciation.approximation: 'gil-ga-MESH' — three even, heavy syllables; the final 'sh' is soft, like sand through fingers.

kin.label: Sumerian
kin.form: Bilgames (Bil₃-ga-mes₃), the older form of the name, interpreted as 'the old man became young'

kin.label: Akkadian
kin.form: Gilgameš, the standard form of the epic's language — the name the epic itself echoes in its plant of youth

kin.label: Learned tradition
kin.form: written with the divine determinative in later texts — the hero reckoned among the gods and a judge of the dead

pronunciation.note: Gilgameš is Tier 1 by the non-Greek rule: the restoration preserves the caron š, a distinctive letter the ASCII 'Gilgamesh' loses along with its redundant h. The name is Sumerian at root; the Akkadian epic made it the most famous royal name of Mesopotamia.

domains.title: The King Who Sought the Deep
domains.subtitle: Kingship, Friendship, and the Quest Against Death
domains.lead: Gilgameš, king of Uruk, 'two-thirds god and one-third man', is the hero of the oldest great epic we possess. He builds walls, slays the guardian of the Cedar Forest, spurns a goddess, loses his friend, and walks to the end of the world to ask the flood's survivor the only question that matters: must we die?

cards.name: King of Uruk
cards.desc: The epic opens and closes on the walls he built — 'go up on the wall of Uruk and walk around' — kingship as masonry.

cards.name: The Friend
cards.desc: Enkidu, the wild man fashioned from clay to match him; their friendship is the first great love story of literature.

cards.name: The Cedar Journey
cards.desc: The road west to the Cedar Forest and the slaying of Humbaba, its monstrous guardian — fame won at the price of doom.

cards.name: The Flood and the Plant
cards.desc: Utnapishtim's ark, the waters of death, and the plant 'the old man becomes young', stolen by a serpent while the king slept.

symbols.name: The wild bull
symbols.meaning: His own title — the goring wild bull, son of Lugalbanda and the goddess Ninsun

symbols.name: The walls of Uruk
symbols.meaning: His true immortality, named in the epic's first and last lines

symbols.name: The cedar
symbols.meaning: The timber of the Cedar Forest, cut for the great door of Uruk

symbols.name: The plant of youth
symbols.meaning: 'The old man becomes young' — rejuvenation won from the sea's floor and lost to the serpent

symbols.name: The deluge
symbols.meaning: The flood of Utnapishtim, the deep he alone among men saw and survived to tell

mythology.lead: The Standard Babylonian epic, 'He who saw the deep', runs from the streets of Uruk to the waters of death. Its twelve tablets hold the first full arc of friendship, loss, and wisdom in world literature.

myths.title: Enkidu Comes from the Wild
myths.text: Uruk groans under its restless young king, and the gods answer by fashioning Enkidu from clay — a wild man who runs with gazelles and frees the trapper's game. The harlot Šamhat civilizes him with bread and beer; he comes to Uruk and blocks Gilgameš at the wedding-house door. They wrestle until the doorframe shakes, and the struggle ends in embrace: from that day the king has a second self.

myths.title: The Cedar Forest and Humbaba
myths.text: Hungry for a lasting name, Gilgameš proposes the expedition to the Cedar Forest, where the monstrous Humbaba guards the trees for the god Enlil. Through dream-omens and terror the two friends go on; with the aid of Šamaš's thirteen winds they bring Humbaba down and fell the great cedar. The glory is real — and fatal. For this, and for the spurned Ištar's Bull of Heaven, the gods decree that one of the two must die: Enkidu sickens, and dies.

myths.title: Across the Waters of Death
myths.text: Clothed in a lion's skin, Gilgameš wanders beyond the world: through the twin mountain where scorpion-men guard the sun's road, along the tunnel of darkness to the garden of jeweled trees, to Šiduri the ale-wife, who tells him what every wisdom text will say after her — eat, drink, hold your child's hand. He crosses the waters of death with the ferryman Ur-šanabi and finds Utnapishtim, the flood's survivor, who tells him the story of the ark and sets him the test of staying awake. He fails.

myths.title: The Old Man Becomes Young
myths.text: Utnapishtim gives him one last chance: a thorny plant at the bottom of the sea, 'the old man becomes young'. Gilgameš ties stones to his feet, dives, and wins it — then stops to bathe at a pool, and a serpent smells the plant, takes it, and sheds its skin. The king sits down and weeps. Then he returns to Uruk, brings Ur-šanabi up onto the wall, and shows him the brickwork: this, the epic says, is what a man leaves.

lore.syncretism: The epic itself was an international text: copies in Akkadian, Hittite, and Hurrian lay in the archives of Hattusa, and scribes from Ashur to Ugarit learned it by heart. Its flood story adapts the older Atra-ḫasīs epic and stands, at a further remove, behind the biblical account of Noah — George Smith's reading of the eleventh tablet in 1872 caused a sensation for exactly that reason. Gilgameš lived on in the margins of later religions: a judge of the dead in Mesopotamian incantations and visions of the netherworld, and, astonishingly, a named giant in the Book of Giants known from Qumran and from Manichaean fragments, where Humbaba's name survives as Ḥobabish.
lore.culturalLegacy: Rediscovered in the ruins of Nineveh, Gilgameš became the measure of how old literature is: every generation since 1872 has re-translated him, from scholarly editions to novels and graphic retellings. He anchors the modern study of the flood traditions, of heroic friendship, and of the wisdom genre. Uruk — Warka in Iraq, a UNESCO World Heritage site — still raises its walls where the epic begins and ends. To write Gilgameš with the caron is a small act of philological justice: the š is the sound of the epic's own language, and the ASCII 'sh' is a translator's patch.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The epic of Gilgameš begins with a wall and ends with a wall, and between them lies the whole education of a human being. At first the king believes what strong young kings believe: that the enemy is distance — the Cedar Forest, the far shore, the undying man beyond the sea. Each victory over distance only brings the real enemy closer, until it stands in his own bedchamber: the fact that he will die. The scorpion-men, the ale-wife, the ferryman, and the flood-hero all tell him the same thing in different voices, and he cannot hear it until the serpent takes the plant. Only then, weeping at the water's edge, does he become the hero of wisdom rather than of strength.

What he brings home is not immortality but an account: 'he who saw the deep' — the epic's first line names him by what he saw and reported, not by what he kept. The plant was for the body; the tale is for the city. And so the last gesture of the poem is a tour of masonry: here are the walls, the brickwork, the threshold. Four thousand years have proven the bargain fair. Uruk's walls are dust, but the tale has outlasted every cedar, every serpent, and every king who heard it and was, for a moment, less afraid.
lore.archaeology: The epic's text is archaeology's gift: the fullest copies are the twelve tablets from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (seventh century BCE), excavated in the nineteenth century and held by the British Museum, where George Smith read the flood tablet in 1872. Behind them lie Old Babylonian fragments (the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets), Middle Babylonian copies from Ugarit and Emar, translations from Hattusa in Anatolia, and, oldest of all, the Sumerian Bilgames poems from Nippur and Ur. The historical kernel is modest but real: the Sumerian King List names Gilgameš as fifth king of the First Dynasty of Uruk, and the vast walls of Uruk (Warka, Iraq) still stand where the epic says he built them.
